content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies how to efficiently perform model stealing in a data-free manner. Specifically, the authors notice that a high diversity of the query dataset, which is measured by entropy, would correspond to a strong model strealing performance. Based on this observation, the authors design a novel efficient data-free model stealing algorithm named DB-DFMS. The DB-DFMS algorithm consists of a generator for synthesizing query datasets and a clone model that aims to clone the functionality of the victim. In each iteration, DB-DFMS will first update the generator in order to maximize the diversity of the synthesized dataset (w.r.t. the current clone model), and then generate a query dataset of high diversity to query the victim and update the clone model. Experiments are conducted on vision datasets to verify the effectiveness of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengh:

1. This paper is well-written and easy to follow.

2. The proposed DB-DFMS method is well-motivated.


Weaknesses (concerns):

1. The proposed DB-DFMS method achieves the same attack performance as that of the existing DFMS-SL method. However, the training time of DB-DFMS is extremely shorter than that of DFMS-SL. I am wondering why this happened, and if it is the case that the long training time of DFMS-SL is inevitable. Therefore, I suggest the authors give a more detailed comparison between their proposed algorithm and DFMS-SL.

2. From Fig. 5 in Section 4.5 and Fig. 7 in Appendix C, it can be found that the synthesized query data contain little semantic information. However, it seems to contradict the intuition that strong model stealing performance requires high-quality (high-semantic) query data. Can the authors give some (intuitive) explanations about this "contradictory"?

3. From Table 2, it can be found that DB-DFMS could not outperform the existing approaches on SVHN and CelebA datasets.
This may partially be due to that model stealing on SVHN and CelebA datasets are easy tasks (in which even the random-noise strategy can achieve acceptable stealing performance). Therefore, to justify the superiority of DB-DFMS, I suggest the authors conduct more experiments on some "harder" datasets, e.g., CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet.

4. I wonder how the stealing performance of DB-DFMS will be when some model stealing defense methods [r1,r2,r3] present.

[r1] Juuti et al. "PRADA: Protecting against DNN model stealing attacks". IEEE SP 2019.

[r2] Kariyappa et al. "Defending against model stealing attacks with adaptive misinformation". CVPR 2021.

[r3] Orekondy et al. "Prediction poisoning: Towards defenses against DNN model stealing attacks". ICLR 2020.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper is well-written and easy to follow. The proposed mehtod is well-motivated and novel, but has not been comprehensively evaluated.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper is well-written and the proposed DB-DFMS method is well-motivated.
However, the empirical evaluation is not comprehensive enough to justify the effectiveness of DB-DFMS.
Therefore, I tend to reject this paper for now.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors show the importance of diversifying the data generated during the data-free model extraction. Specifically, the generator in data-free model extraction is forced to create various images across all the classes. The new simplified framework, called diversity-based data-free model stealing (DB-DFMS), is shown to improve the attack performance and decrease the required query budget as compared to the previous work, especially DFME.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

1. The authors consider relevant baselines.

Weaknesses:

1. According to Table 2 - the newly proposed method does not outperform the previous ones DFME and DFMS-SL in terms of performance on SVHN, CIFAR10, and CelebA datasets. The train time is very similar to DFME.

Comments:

Comments
- "Concretely, we take advantage of the generative models and force the generator to generate various images across all the classes, and our general hypothesis is that such images contain more information which can better represent the victim model’s data distribution and thus enhance the attack performance" - This attack assumes that the public API exposes all possible classes. 
- Not only data diversity is required but also the examples should be chosen that are with the highest disagreement against the already stolen copy. Thus, this work shows only a single side of the stealing process. 
- The attack setting on page 5 is the same as for DFME, which should be mentioned, from: "We choose 2M query budget for SVHN and 20M for CIFAR-10" 
- Some of the conclusions from experiments are rather trivial and should be omitted in the main part of the paper, for instance: "Figure 2. As we can see, all the attack performance has a positive correlation to the query budget,"

Questions:
- How many queries are used for the experiments in Table 1?
- What is the intuition behind the fact that random noise achieves lower entropy than natural data?

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
- The paper tackles the problem of data-free model stealing attack (i.e., to clone a black-box model without any assumptions on its training data).
- It builds on top of the existing attack framework of Kariyappa et al., 2021 and Truong et al., 2021 - by iterating over (a) training a generator model to synthesize query images and (b) training a clone model to mimic the black-box victim model on the set of synthesized images. 
- The key contribution of the paper is examining the importance of label diversity -- the proposed approach achieves this by encouraging the generator model to synthesize images which result in high-entropy predictions.
- Evaluations on SVHN, CelebA, CIFAR10 indicates that the results of the proposed approach is on-par with recent approaches.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths

**1. Relevant properties of query images**
- Within the data-free model stealing framework, previous works (e.g., DFME) have largely addressed what makes for a *good gradient signal* to update the generator model. I appreciate that this paper studies a complementary direction -- instead of the gradient signal, it studies actually makes for a *good query dataset* produced by the generator model. 

**2. Evaluation**
- The evaluation in the paper is broad -- it analyzes various factors e.g., t-SNE representations of the produced embeddings, comparing entropy of multiple baseline approaches.

### Concerns

**1. (Major concern) Evidence to support argument of diversity**
- If I understand right, the paper specifically studies the role of *label* diversity (and not diversity among other things such as low-level or semantic features in query images) -- I recommend the authors to make this more precise in the claims.
- More generally, the claim of the paper is that label diversity (measured in terms of entropy over predicted probabilities) is a "critical factor in model stealing". I find this claim has a few problems:
- (a) this applies only in the case of a known prior over class labels. In the case of the balanced datasets used in the paper, this is essentially a uniform prior and hence label diversity is naturally important. In fact, authors explicitly construct some test scenarios to have balanced classes (e.g., CelebA); and
- (b) I don't think this claim generally holds. A simple counter-example I can think of is taking a poor surrogate set of query images (e.g., random noise images to steal CIFAR-10) and adversarially perturbing them to achieve maximum label diversity. Since we only further add uninformative information to random noise images, I hypothesize this results in high-entropy (which paper claims is critical for model stealing), but low model stealing accuracy contradicting the paper's claim;
- (c) The above is also supported by Figure 4 - approaches with low entropy (e.g., DFME) achieves performance on-par with the proposed high-entropy approach. 
- Overall, it appears that there is not enough evidence in the paper (or also sometimes counter-evidence) to support that label diversity is essential to improving performance.

**2. (Major concern) Significance of findings**
- I also find it difficult to find the exact significance of the empirical results. Although the proposed approach claims diversity is important, it achieves comparable results to baselines (mostly on-par with them across all datasets).
- Moreover, in spite of a explicit loss to encourage diversity in the proposed approach, it appears that other relevant baselines obtains higher diversity -- for instance, DFMS-SL has higher entropy in all cases compared to the proposed approach.
- Perhaps the authors could consider training the generator with both the diversity loss along with some approximate gradient estimate from previous approaches (in other words, add the diversity loss term to losses of previous approaches). 

**3. (Minor concern) Writing**
- Table 1: What was the query budget for which the accuracy was obtained?
- (nitpicks) Many odd phrases or typos: "performance of DenseNet-121 is awesome", "has drew huge attention", "even shows the superiority", "its specific designing"
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity**: Good. The paper is overall quite easy to read. The technical details are well written and is well-positioned with relevant literature. The only nitpick I have are many odd phrases and typos (see concern 3), but this didn't particular impact clarity in my opinion.

**Quality**: Below Average. I find that the claims in the paper are not rigorously supported (see concern 1), or sometimes are also disproved during evaluation.

**Novelty**: Below Average. The only technical novelty in the paper appears to simply replace the approximate gradient estimate in previous works with an entropy term. While there is some empirical analysis, there is little insight to accompany the technical innovation.

**Reproducibility**: Good. Although code is not provided, I am somewhat confident in reproducing the results based on the descriptions in Sec. 4.1 and Appendix A.
content.summary_of_the_review: I think the paper studies a a relevant insight - the role of diverse features (labels in this case) in synthetic query images for model stealing. However, I find that the claim is insufficiently supported in the paper (e.g., results are on-par with "non-diverse" baselines, some of which seem to have better diversity).
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper is in the model stealing area. The thesis is that keeping the generated data samples diverse across all the classes improves attack performance.  The authors claim advantages in attack efficiency and query budget. They propose a technique called DB-DFMS that forces the generator to generate examples across all the classes. 

More concretely, for training the generator, they use negative entropy as the diversity loss and attempt to minimize that. And for training the clone model, they minimize the KL-divergence between the victim and the clone model. 

The authors provide performance comparisons with several prior schemes. 

The idea of including diversity in model stealing is not entirely new. See https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/stamp/stamp.jsp?tp=&arnumber=9880326 for one paper at 2022 CVPR.    Their loss formulation appears to be essentially identical to that proposed by the authors (see equations (5) and (6) in the 2022 CVPR paper versus equation (2) in the current paper).  So, key claim to novelty at the conceptual is lost.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 
-- The idea of diversity-based loss was potentially interesting, but  prior work potentially renders it no longer novel. It seems that the CVPR 2022 paper had the same idea on diversity-based loss, but went further in some ways.  The authors may have to figure out what is novel in light of that paper and reposition their work.


Weaknesses: 

-- CVPR 2022 paper by Sanyal et al. titled "Towards Data-Free Model Stealing in a Hard Label Setting" proposes a similar diversity loss function for model stealing. The authors need to address that if that is used in soft-label setting (rather than hard-label) to make a fair comparison.

-- Another CVPR 2022 paper appears to use a very similar loss function for updating the generator. A comparison with that is also needed.  It seems the citation to this work is also missing.

https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2022/papers/Zhang_Towards_Efficient_Data_Free_Black-Box_Adversarial_Attack_CVPR_2022_paper.pdf

-- How does the scheme compare with MAZE in terms of performance? 

-- I would also recommend including a performance comparison with the CVPR 2022 technique.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is generally well-written, but missing recent related work (especially a better comparison with the two CVPR 2022 papers, one of which is not cited).  It needs to compare with that.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper proposes an interesting idea, but unfortunately, the same loss function is used  in CVPR 2022 Sanyal et al. So, the main claim to novelty is lost. The authors may need to figure out the novelty or better present it in light of that work and reposition their work. Comparisons are also needed with that work under the same assumptions (e.g., soft-label setting).

Minor quibbles: 

In Table 3, I I wonder if comparing on run-time is a reasonable strategy without micro-benchmarks of some sort.  All the schemes had the same query budget. So, the run-time differences  need to be explored more in-depth so as to be sure they are not due to optimization (or lack of)  of the code. The run-differences between DFME and DB-DFMS vary from about 1.5% to 6%. That may also need to be elaborated -- what overhead is coming from queries and what portion from outside that. Putting aside fixed overhead from queries  may also better highlight the performance gains with DB-DFMS.
